target: AG1’s claim that school dissection mostly uses already-dead animals and meat-industry byproducts
objection: AG2 argues that the way dissection animals are supplied is inhumane, environmentally harmful, and largely involves animals caught in the wild, so classroom dissection should be seen as harming animals and biodiversity rather than merely repurposing dead byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally valuable enough to justify continued use
objection: AG2 says the educational and scientific goals of biology classes and medical training can be met without animal dissection, because standards such as AP Biology and NGSS do not require it and medical schools do not use animals for physician training.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives are inferior to real dissection
objection: AG2 contends that synthetic models and computer simulations teach anatomy equally well or better, so animal dissection is unnecessary because students can learn just as well with alternatives.

target: AG2’s inference from medical-school/standards non-use to the conclusion that school biology needs no dissection
objection: AG1 objects that medical training objectives are different from school biology objectives, so the fact that medical schools or certain standards do not require dissection does not show that school biology goals can be met without it.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection harms animals and biodiversity through wild capture
objection: AG1 argues that if schools use already-dead animals or byproducts, then school dissection does not meaningfully drive wild-capture or local biodiversity loss, because the harm chain depends on obtaining live wild animals for specimens.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives teach just as well as real dissection
objection: AG1 objects that synthetic models and computer simulations are simplified and standardized, lack the tactile properties of real tissues, and do not capture anatomical variability, so they generally provide less embodied learning than real specimens.

target: AG2’s claim that medical-school/standards non-use proves dissection is unnecessary in biology education
objection: AG1 says that the absence of animal dissection in medical training or some standards does not determine what school biology educational goals require, because those settings have different objectives.

target: AG2’s claim that school dissection does not need live animals and therefore can be rejected on welfare grounds
objection: AG1 argues that using appropriately sourced dead or byproduct specimens means the animals were not killed for the lesson, so the dissection makes educational use of animals already produced by industry rather than causing new animal deaths.

target: AG2’s claim that most dissection animals are wild-caught and therefore school dissection harms biodiversity
objection: AG1 says most dissection specimens are already deceased and that wild-capture is therefore not a plausible description of how specimens reach schools, so the biodiversity-harm chain is not established.

target: AG2’s broader claim that school dissection harms animals and biodiversity
objection: AG1 argues that appropriately sourced dead/byproduct specimens are already destined for disposal and that using them for education imposes little or no incremental animal harm or biodiversity harm compared with not using them.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct use avoids biodiversity harm
objection: AG2 replies that the claim is false because typical school dissection allegedly still relies on wild-caught animals, so the biodiversity-harm pathway is present in practice rather than absent.

target: AG1’s claim that dead/byproduct sourcing removes the core harms of dissection
objection: AG2 contends that even if some specimens are described as byproducts, typical dissection still depends on an inhumane wild-capture supply chain, so appropriate-byproduct sourcing does not eliminate the central harms.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives are not equivalent to dissection
objection: AG2 says the educational goals of school biology can be met without dissection because standards do not require it and computer/synthetic alternatives teach anatomy effectively, at least as well as or better than real animal dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection with dead/byproduct specimens eliminates the inhumane aspects of specimen acquisition
objection: AG2 argues that avoiding wild capture does not eliminate the inhumane and environmentally harmful aspects of sourcing specimens for dissection, so the practice remains objectionable even with byproducts.

target: AG2’s claim that byproduct sourcing is still inhumane and environmentally harmful
objection: AG1 responds that if schools use appropriately sourced dead/byproduct specimens, they do not need to kill or capture animals for the lesson, so the inhumane aspects tied to live capture are avoided.

target: AG1’s claim that permitting dissection only repurposes waste and does not create new harms
objection: AG2 argues that if schools permit dissection, they must keep buying specimens, which increases demand upstream; therefore permitting dissection contributes to more procurement of specimens rather than merely using a fixed waste stream.

target: AG2’s claim that permitting dissection increases upstream harm through demand
objection: AG1 counters that meat-industry byproducts are generated as part of normal processing, not because schools demand them, so using them for dissection mainly repurposes existing material rather than driving new killing or capture.

target: AG1’s claim that death/byproduct sourcing means the lesson does not require killing or capturing animals
objection: AG2 argues that if most dissection animals are wild-caught, then specimen supply chains typically do involve newly capturing live animals for dissection, which means schools do end up obtaining animals by killing or capturing them for the lesson.
